howto.h1: URL to Video: turn a product link into a video ad
howto.lead: Paste one product URL — AI imports the photos and details for you, then turns them into a ready-to-post video. No camera, no filming, no editing timeline.

image.alt: Canvas tote bag product photo on a white background

intro: Most sellers start with one live product page and no video budget. URL to Video reads that page, keeps the title, the description and the photos you already published, and opens a prefilled product-demo draft. No camera, no clips.

The path suits a listing already good enough to sell from. If the photos are the weak part, improve them first. The importer can only work with what the page shows, so a thin listing produces a thin draft.

Nothing about the import is fixed in place. You correct the copy, choose the photo the video opens on, and describe the demo in your words. Building the draft costs nothing; the price of the video appears after you review it.

sections.h2: Where the link path saves time
paras: A working product page already answers what a script has to answer: what the item is, who it suits, and why a buyer would choose it. The importer turns those answers into the first draft, so you review instead of compose.

Take a different start when the page is not the bottleneck. A single strong shot moves faster through [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video), and a product with no page yet belongs in [Text to Video](/guides/how-do-text-to-video). Sellers planning many videos keep every import in [Product Links](/guides/how-do-product-links) instead.

sections.h2: What the importer needs from the page
paras: The link must be public and served over https. Pages behind a login, a cart gate or a regional block do not open for the reader, and the tool returns a specific reason rather than a blank draft. That reason tells you what to fix.

Good input is a listing a stranger could buy from: a clear title, a description with real detail, and photos large enough to survive a vertical crop. One thumbnail and a single line of copy give the draft almost nothing to shape.
bullets: A page that opens in a browser without signing in.
A title that names the product rather than a campaign.
Photos big enough that the product still reads on a phone.
Variants written as text, not locked inside an image.

sections.h2: Checking what the import read
paras: The preview returns four things: the sourced title, the description, the images it detected, and a possible price. Each carries a confidence label, so you can tell a clean read from a guess. Read all four before you brief anything.

A possible price stays a hint and is never treated as confirmed. The reader may pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line, and nothing checks it. If the ad shows a number, type the one you stand behind.

sections.h2: Confirming cost and starting the job
paras: One click on the imported entry opens the prefilled draft in the composer, with the photos, the description and the format settings already in place. Add a sentence of direction, then read the estimate.

A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40. The confirmation modal restates that cost and your balance; confirming holds the credits. A failed job returns them, and the job runs on the server.

sections.h2: Where the finished video goes
paras: Finished work lands in the Library under All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed. The details modal shows the result, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution.

When one clip is wrong, pick the smallest repair. Try again re-runs a failed job, Retry render re-assembles clips that are already fine, and Regenerate prefills the composer from the job. Captions are a separate pass in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), and each pass saves a new version.

sections.h2: How to import a product page into your first draft
paras: Start at your workspace Home and paste the link to a public product page. The import reads that link and usually brings back a main product shot, a model shot and an in-use shot, plus the title, the description, the detected price and the product details. It also writes a first draft of the video, so you start with a structure rather than a blank brief.

Nothing is charged until you have read what the import returned. The imported photos and fields land in the tool tab, where you can fix anything the page did not carry, such as a size, a color name or a short description. Once the brief reads right, the credit estimate appears before you confirm, and confirming reserves those credits. A job that fails hands them back.

steps.title: Paste the product link
steps.body: Open [Home](/app/create/home) and paste the link to the product page into the field at the top. Use a public product page rather than a private account screen, so the import can read it. Once the link is in, you continue in the tool tab, where the import begins and the photos and copy start to fill in.

steps.title: Review what the import found
steps.body: In the tool tab, the import lists the photos it found, often a plain product shot, a model shot and an in-use shot. Below them sit the title, the description, the detected price and the product details. Read each one against the real product and note anything that looks wrong, such as a color name or a price that no longer matches the page.

steps.title: Correct the details by hand
steps.body: Move to the composer and edit the fields the import left thin. If the page carried no size, type the tote measurements or a short line such as heavy canvas with two handles. Rewrite the title in plain words and trim the description to two sentences. Save the draft when the fields read right, since saving generates nothing and spends no credits.

steps.title: Brief the video in the composer
steps.body: The import has already written a first draft, so read it before you change it. Keep the shot order if it makes sense, then rewrite the lines that describe the product: what appears in the first three seconds, the scene, the framing and the sound. Adjust the duration and the aspect ratio on the same screen, and leave the draft saved if you want to stop here.

steps.title: Confirm the estimate and generate
steps.body: The composer shows the credit estimate before anything runs. Read it next to the duration and the shot count, then open the confirmation dialog. Confirming reserves the credits for this job. If the number looks high, step back and cut a shot or shorten the duration before you confirm. A job that fails returns its credits automatically, so you can try again.

steps.title: Collect the file from the Library
steps.body: When the render finishes, open [the Library](/app/create/library) and find the job under your finished files. Play it once at full size before you download, checking the product photo against the real tote. Download the file and post it, or send it to Subtitle Studio first if you want captions. The file stays downloadable for 15 days and carries no watermark.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: The loop matches the rest of the workspace: supply the source, review what was read, confirm a cost, then wait for a server job. The difference here is that a link carries the photos and the description for you.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Guests can build the draft without an account, and it is restored the moment they sign in. Save as draft costs nothing, so compare two directions before spending credits.

checklist: The product page opens in a browser without signing in.
The description on the page matches what you actually sell.
You chose the shot the video opens on, not the first one listed.
The price in the copy is one you typed, not the imported guess.
You read the estimate before confirming, not after.

faq.q: Does the product page need anything special?
faq.a: It needs to be public and served over https. The reader takes the title, the description, the photos and a possible price from the page. A page behind a login returns a specific reason instead of a draft.

faq.q: What if the import picks a photo I don't want?
faq.a: Deselect it before you brief the video, then choose the shot the video opens on from the ones you keep. The video is built only from those photos. A wide lifestyle image often crops down to an empty frame.

faq.q: How much does one video cost?
faq.a: The composer shows the estimated credits before anything runs. A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40, and the confirmation modal restates the cost and your balance. A failed job returns the credits.

faq.q: What happens to the price the importer found?
faq.a: It stays a possible price, marked with a confidence label, and it is never treated as confirmed. The reader can pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line. Type the figure you want in the ad.

howto.h1: Image to Video: bring one product photo to life
howto.lead: Upload a single product photo and add a short prompt — watch the photo come alive as a moving product clip, ready for ads and social posts.

image.alt: Peachy tinted balm product photo on a marble vanity

intro: You already have the product photo. You need a few seconds where it moves: a hand lifting the bottle, a cap twisting open, light sliding across a label. Image to Video turns that photo and one action into a clip you can post.

The photo supplies the look: colours, surface, background. You supply the action in one short sentence. The camera drift, the pace, how firmly the product keeps its shape: the model decides. That is why the photo matters more than wording.

Upload, describe, confirm, compare: the loop is short and it repeats. Slow down on the first two, since a clean photo and one verb do more than any rewrite. If your product exists only as a page link, start with [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video).

sections.h2: What a single photo can do
paras: Image to Video suits products that read as one object: a balm tin, a tumbler, a folded shirt. The photo holds still while the model moves around it, so what you sell stays recognisable as motion arrives.

Some jobs want another tool. A page link is faster through URL to Video, which imports listing photos. Several angles in one longer story belong in AI Video, which takes up to four photos. A product that needs a speaker belongs in [AI Avatar](/guides/how-do-ai-avatar).

sections.h2: What makes a photo workable
paras: The composer accepts up to four product reference photos, and one is usually enough. The model needs a subject it can separate from its surroundings, so it moves the camera without smearing your product's edges.

Plain backgrounds win. A crowded shelf makes the model guess which shape is yours; a wall removes the guess. Even light keeps the label readable. A phone photo counts, since motion comes from your sentence, and the [product photo field guide](/guides/product-photo-tips) covers lighting in depth.
bullets: One product filling a third to half the frame.
Plain background, so nothing competes with the product.
Even light from one side so the label reads.
A phone shot at normal zoom, unfiltered and uncropped.

sections.h2: The quote before the job runs
paras: Before anything runs, the composer shows the cost. A 15-second clip costs 20 credits, a 30-second clip costs 40, and the figure changes with the duration. Set the length first, then read the line.

Choosing between them is a placement question. Fifteen seconds carries one beat for half the credits, which suits a test of a new angle. Thirty buys a second beat, a close-up then a use, if something real goes there.
The confirmation modal restates the estimated cost and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them automatically. The job runs on the server, so you can leave the page.

sections.h2: Reading the motion you got
paras: Watch the clip twice. First with sound off, as a scroller would meet it; then with your attention on the product. One pass says whether the motion reads, the other whether the label survived.

One motion per clip keeps results clean. Two actions in one brief, pick up and pour, split the model's attention and land neither. When a story needs both beats, make two clips and keep the stronger take.
When a result is close but wrong, a variation beats a rewrite. Change one thing, the verb, the photo or the duration, then compare both takes. Two changes at once hide which one fixed it.
bullets: Wrong action: rewrite the verb and regenerate the clip.
Odd pacing: try the brief at the other length.
Product deforming: swap the photo, not the sentence.
Flat framing: keep the take, change the angle later.

sections.h2: Where the clip goes next
paras: Finished videos wait in the Library, where All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed separate running jobs from ready ones. The badge updates while you are away. Download what you keep within 15 days.

The details modal lists the duration, aspect ratio and resolution you submitted, plus every reference you attached. If the clip needs words, [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio) works on completed videos and saves each pass as a version. Run the [review checklist](/blog/ai-video-review-checklist) first.

sections.h2: How one product photo becomes a clip for any platform
paras: Image to Video starts from a still you already have. Upload one product photo, describe the motion you want in a short prompt, and the tool returns a moving clip that keeps the product readable. You don't book a shoot or hire anyone to hold the item, so a photo taken on a kitchen table can open an ad. When you want to try it, [open the workspace](/app/create).

Three directions are documented for the same photo. A creator-style TikTok unboxing opens on a strong hook and walks through the product, an Instagram get-ready reel sits in soft light with minimal captions, and a Facebook offer testimonial leads with the deal and shows the item in use. All three are 9:16 vertical, 10-second loops. Review the generated details against the photo before you publish, and if you only have a link, [import the product page instead](/guides/how-do-url-to-video).

cards.body: Opens on a strong hook, then walks through the product step by step. The framing stays creator-style, so it reads like a first look rather than a finished ad. Your upload supplies the item.

cards.title: Instagram: get-ready reel
cards.body: Soft light, a measured pace and minimal captions. The reel follows a routine built around the product rather than a hard sell. Keep the colors true to the photo as the clip moves.
cards.meta: get-ready reel, soft light, minimal captions

cards.title: Facebook: offer testimonial
cards.body: Leads with the deal, then shows the product in use so the offer has proof. The testimonial framing carries the message without a hard sell. Compare the generated details with your photo before publishing.

steps.title: Upload the product photo in Home
steps.body: Home is where a new product starts, so upload the photo there first. A clear shot such as a canvas tote bag on a wooden table works better than a busy scene, because the tool needs the item's edges and color to read. Once the upload finishes you see the photo attached, and the next click takes you to the tool tab you chose from the tools menu.

steps.title: Pick Image to Video in the tool tab
steps.body: The tool tab opens with that photo already attached, and the prompt field sits in front of you. This is the point to decide which of the three documented directions you want, because each one sets a different tone for the prompt you write next. The format controls and the estimate area stay on the same screen, so nothing is hidden behind a second page.

steps.title: Write the motion prompt in the composer
steps.body: In the composer, describe the motion in plain words: a slow push toward the tote, a hand lifting it from the table, a turn that shows the other side. Name the light you want and keep the original framing as the base shot. Set the aspect to 9:16 and the duration to 10 seconds when you are aiming at one of the documented placements.

steps.title: Confirm the credit estimate
steps.body: The confirmation dialog shows the credit estimate before anything is rendered. Read the number, check the aspect and duration once more, then confirm to reserve the credits. A failed job returns those credits automatically, so a misfire does not eat the budget. If something looks off, close the dialog and fix it in the composer before you confirm.

steps.title: Compare the clip with your photo
steps.body: Generation runs and the clip lands in the job view. Play it beside the original photo and compare shape, color and any logo, so the item still reads as the same product. If a detail drifted, open Regenerate, which prefills the composer from the job so you change one line instead of rewriting the whole brief.

steps.title: Download the file from the Library
steps.body: Finished clips sit in the Library next to your drafts and versions, and they stay downloadable for 15 days. Open the job, download the file, and note that the download carries no watermark. For a second platform, use Regenerate to prefill the composer from this job, adjust the prompt, then confirm the new estimate before you render again.

stepsIntro.title: Six steps, one photo
stepsIntro.lead: The loop is short: one photo, one sentence, one confirmed job. Most of the thinking happens before you click, in choosing the photo and narrowing the action to a single motion.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: If the action feels wrong but the framing is right, change the verb before the photo. Rewriting one word costs less than reshooting and isolates the cause of a miss.

checklist: Product fully in frame on a plain or blurred background.
One verb in the action line, no second beat.
Duration chosen before you read the cost line.
Confirmation modal cost and balance matching what you expect.
Clip watched once with sound off before you download it.

faq.q: What kind of photo works best?
faq.a: One clear product, a plain background and even light. A phone photo is enough, since motion comes from the action you write rather than the source file.

faq.q: How long can the clip be?
faq.a: Choose 15 or 30 seconds when you set up the job. The composer shows 20 credits for fifteen seconds and 40 for thirty. Start short when testing a new angle.

faq.q: Can I use the clip in ads?
faq.a: Yes. Download the finished file from the Library with no watermark, then use it on your product page, in social posts and in paid ads. Publishing to TikTok or Meta takes one click.

faq.q: What happens if the motion comes out wrong?
faq.a: Regenerate with one change: a clearer verb, a cleaner photo or the other duration. Two takes show which input caused the miss. If a job fails, the reason is in plain language and the credits return automatically.

intro: Text to Video turns a short description of your product into a shooting script you can edit. You type one or two lines, press the Optimize button, and the composer hands back scenes, shots and a voice lined up as a brief.

Nothing renders while you read that brief. Every line stays editable, from the opening shot to the closing words, and the price appears once you settle on a version. Most first drafts need one pass to sharpen the claim and one to cut a repeating shot.
Reach for this tool when you have a product and a point to make, but no script. If photos or a product page already exist, a sibling tool saves the typing.

sections.h2: Where a sentence beats a photo
paras: Text to Video suits a claim you can say out loud: a serum that calms redness, a mat that stays put through a sprint. The brief supplies the shot order, the on-screen words and the voice. Photos can ground the scenes, but they never replace the sentence.

Pick a different tab when the raw material already exists. [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video) starts from one to four product photos and keeps the item in frame; [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video) reads a public HTTPS product page and builds the brief from it. AI Image returns stills inline.

sections.h2: The sentence that starts everything
paras: Name three things in one or two lines: the product, the person you are talking to, and the single message they should leave with. A line carrying all three gives the composer a structure to fill. A slogan gives it nothing.

Compare "Give this moisturizer an honest review" with "Great results, amazing product". The first names an item, a tone and a job. The second could sit under any product on any shelf, so the scenes come back generic.
bullets: Product first: the exact item, not the category.
Audience second: who is deciding and what they already believe.
One message last: the claim the video has to land.
Leave out adjectives that would fit any competitor.

sections.h2: What you set before the quote
paras: Five controls decide what you pay for and what comes back: the Type selector, then model, aspect ratio, duration and resolution. Set them before you press Optimize, because each one shapes the brief the composer writes.

Then the quote. The confirmation window restates the estimated cost and your balance, and confirming holds the credits while the job runs. A failed job returns them automatically, with a plain-language reason and a Try again button. Save as draft costs nothing if the brief can wait.
bullets: Type keeps the job on Text to Video rather than a reference tab.
Aspect ratio decides the frame your shots are composed inside.
Duration sets the script length: 15 seconds costs 20 credits, 30 seconds costs 40.
Resolution sets how much detail the file keeps when it is re-cut.

sections.h2: Judging the result shot by shot
paras: Open the details modal for the finished video, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution. The per-shot clips show which scene missed, instead of letting the whole edit take the blame.

intro: AI Video turns the product photos you already own into a short clip of a scene you describe. Attach them, write one moment, and the composer builds video where the product keeps its shape, colour and label from first frame to last.

The references do the steering, so this tool suits a product you can photograph from more than one side. A single photo, a plain sentence or a live product page each lead to a different route, and which route fits your material is the first decision.

Plan for two passes, not one. The first take shows you where the description was vague, and the second fixes it. Knowing what each reference steers, and how to word a single scene, usually saves you a whole third pass.

sections.h2: When references should drive the shot
paras: Choose AI Video when the product must look right in every shot: a printed logo, a specific label, a visible sole. You hold photos of it already, and the rest of the scene is what you invent.

Other tools cover different cases. One photo becomes motion in [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video). A public product page is quicker in [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video), which pulls the product pictures for you.

The rule is about what you already hold. Photos from more than one side point here. If most of the clip is a person and the product appears only at the end, description carries the job and [Text to Video](/guides/how-do-text-to-video) is the lighter brief.

sections.h2: What each reference steers
paras: Photos fix the product. Attach one to four; each extra angle gives the model another side to read. Label text, the join of a strap and the taper of a bottle come from those pictures, not from your sentence.

On models that support them, two more slots appear. A reference video steers movement and camera behaviour. A reference audio sample steers the sound, so the take carries a tone. Slots belong to the model, so check them after a switch.
bullets: A product page screenshot leaves the label too soft to read.
A blurry angled phone shot teaches the model the blur as well.
A reference video with a quick cut invites that quick cut back.

sections.h2: A scene the model can finish
paras: One scene means one place, one subject and one thing happening. Name the room and the light, then the action: 'a hallway at eight, sun across the floor, she sets the tote down.' The model picks the camera move and the rhythm.

Leave the camera work out. Writing 'slow push-in, then a cut to the label' spends words on a decision the model makes better from one strong moment. A single action keeps the clip readable; a vague line such as 'show the bag being useful' gives no place, light or action.

sections.h2: What happens after you confirm
paras: Nothing runs until you confirm. The estimated cost appears as you change a reference or a duration: 20 credits for a 15-second video, 40 for 30 seconds. Edit an input and the figure can move, so read it once more before clicking.

The confirmation restates the estimate and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them on its own; the [refunds policy](/refunds) covers the rest. The job runs on the server, so leave the page and the Library badge catches up with "generating", "finishing" and "completed".

note.title: Two kinds of retry
note.body: Use "Retry render" when the clips are fine and only the assembly is wrong. Use "Regenerate" when the take drifted; it refills the composer from the job.

sections.h2: Comparing two takes of one brief
paras: Run the same brief again without editing it, then open both takes in the Library. Watch the opening two seconds and the shot where the product sits closest. Check the label, the strap and the light you asked for.

Open the details modal and the per-shot clips settle it. One weak shot with the rest holding is an assembly problem. A drift across every shot is a brief problem, and the description needs a sharper place or action.

Finished videos stay in the Library for 15 days, so download the keeper the day you choose it. Publish to TikTok or Meta in one click, or download without a watermark and size the crop with [ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform).

paras: The import needs a public HTTPS product page: your own shop, a marketplace listing, or a landing page. It reads the title, description and images already published there, and a price when the page shows one.

A description that names material, size or colour
Page stays public, with no sign-in step
One product per page, not a range in one listing

intro: An AI avatar is a presenter who reads your script on camera without a shoot, a studio or anyone in front of a lens. You attach the product photos, cast the face and voice, and the video comes back with the item in hand.

Not every product needs a voice. A single photo that should move belongs in [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video), and a scene built from several product shots belongs in [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video). Reach for the presenter when the value of the item has to be explained out loud.
Three decisions shape the result: which presenter, which words, which format. None of them is a setting you can fix in the edit. Get them right and the rest is confirmation and waiting.

sections.h2: When a presenter carries the story
paras: A talking presenter suits products that need explaining: why the fabric holds, how the strap adjusts, what fits inside the bag. Casting sets the tone, because a calm delivery suits an everyday product and reads flat on a launch. The face gives the viewer someone to follow while the script sells.

The usual failure is a presenter describing something the viewer cannot see. Small items and dark items need the hands and the placement to do more work, and no voice fixes a product that stays out of frame.

sections.h2: What the workspace asks for
paras: You provide product photos, a presenter and a script. The picker holds 53 available avatars with filters for All, Women and Men, plus search by name, character or scene. Each card previews the voice and a sample line.
Photos decide how the hands look. Send the item alone on a plain surface, with front and back both sharp enough to read on a phone. Two clear angles beat five near identical shots.
bullets: One frame for each side the viewer will see in the cut.
Even light on the product, so the colour holds in the cut.
A close shot of the detail the script points at, so it survives a thumbnail.

sections.h2: From quote to finished job
paras: Your cost appears before anything runs, and the confirmation modal restates the estimate beside your current balance. A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40. Confirming holds the credits until the job settles.

Server-side, the job runs while you do something else. Close the tab if you like, because the Library badge moves from generating to finishing to completed while you are away. A failed render returns the credits automatically, with no support ticket.

note.title: Nothing is spent until it runs
note.body: Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job hands them back. A draft costs nothing and is restored when a guest signs in.

sections.h2: Reading the result honestly
paras: Watch the opening with the sound off, then again with it on. If the product is not visible and in use by the end of the first line, later frames rarely recover the viewer.

Sort the fault before you spend again. A voice that does not fit, a face with the wrong energy, or hands that grip the item badly are casting problems. Another presenter fixes all three. Broken joins are assembly problems, so Retry render re-runs assembly when the clips are sound.
When the words are the fault, Regenerate prefills the composer from the job. That keeps the presenter and the photos in place while you rewrite only the line that failed.

sections.h2: Keeping the file and the cuts
paras: Finished videos sit in the Library for 15 days, then expire, so download what you keep. Filters for All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed sort the list, and the details modal shows the result and every reference you attached.

Keep one presenter for a campaign and test the script instead of the face. A viewer who meets the same person three times recognises the ad before the product name appears, while a new actor each time starts the introduction over.

Captions come after the cut. [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio) works on completed videos only. Each operation saves a new version and leaves the original untouched. Captions from the actual speech follow the delivery, while Product copy puts your own lines on screen.

Upload your product photos and the presenter shows the item you sent, keeping its shape, color and logo true to the photo. intro: Subtitle Studio takes a video you have already finished and gives it captions. Nothing is re-shot: you pick an existing job from the list and the tool writes a second cut beside it. The version you approved stays exactly as it was.

Most feeds play with the sound off, so the caption line is often the only thing a viewer reads before scrolling. A silent autoplay feed turns spoken words into on-screen text. A clip that opens with a line nobody can hear has no argument.

You can caption the speech in the video, or set your own words for each screen. Either way you choose the look, check the sample preview, and keep both cuts. The steps below cover the operations, the style choices, and how to pick the better version.

sections.h2: Captions carry a silent feed
paras: A muted feed removes your voice track and leaves the picture. Viewers still decide within a second whether the clip is for them, and words on screen are the fastest thing to read. Captions turn a spoken line into a visible claim.

Reach for this tool when the footage is settled and the words need work. If the shots are wrong, go back to the composer: the [AI Video guide](/guides/how-do-ai-video) covers a fresh render. Captions repair a silent cut, not a dull one.

sections.h2: What each operation asks of you
paras: Generate subtitles reads the speech in the video and turns it into captions, so you bring nothing but the finished clip. Promo lines and Product copy take text you write, each line becoming one screen. A pasted paragraph arrives as one crowded line.

Good input is short. Write one idea per line, each short enough to read in a breath. Three tight lines beat a full script, and [the AI UGC video ads guide](/blog/ai-ugc-video-ads-guide) shows how an opening works.
bullets: Generate subtitles when the spoken script is already right.
Promo lines for a short hook laid over the footage.
Product copy when on-screen text must name the item.

sections.h2: Preview, then save a version
paras: Pick the video from the list on the left, narrowing it with a word from the prompt or the title. Choose the operation, then set Style, Size, Position, Colour and Backdrop. The sample caption preview updates as you change each control.

Starting the job saves a new version instead of overwriting the file you selected. The original keeps its Library entry and the captioned cut arrives beside it. Leave the page while the job runs; the badge updates when you return.

note.title: One control at a time
note.body: Moving Size, Position and Backdrop together leaves you unsure which one fixed the line. Change one setting, watch the preview, then decide.

sections.h2: A caption that runs past the screen
paras: A line is too long when the preview wraps or reaches the edges before the sentence ends. On a phone the limit is how often the eye jumps back to the start, not the character count. If reading it aloud leaves you behind, the line is long.

Three clean repairs: cut the line to its subject and verb, split it across two screens, or raise Size a step and drop it to the bottom. Change one thing, then watch the preview. Style combinations that hold up stay legible over moving footage.
bullets: Bold with a box backdrop holds up over busy product shots.
White text with an outline survives pale walls and daylight.
Bottom position keeps faces and hands clear on a vertical crop.

sections.h2: Comparing versions before you post
paras: Versions stack as tabs above the player. Switch between them at the same timestamp, sound off, and ask which answers a buyer's first question. A line that reads well on a desktop can vanish into a busy phone frame, so check the crop you will post.

Keep the tab you trust, download it, and publish. Finished videos stay in the Library for 15 days, so download what you want to keep. Crops for each placement sit in [ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform), with [the review checklist](/blog/ai-video-review-checklist) for the rest.

sections.h2: Style, size and position for every caption
paras: Caption work comes last in Subtitle Studio, after the video itself is generated. You don't write the text: it's read from your voiceover automatically, line by line. Your job is the look and the wording. Pick a style, a size, a position and a color that stay readable over the product, then read each line against what's on screen. Open the tool from the menu in the workspace and the settings below are what you see.

Nothing about the video's picture changes — you're only adding words on top. The captioned file is saved as a new version, so the render you already had stays in the Library untouched. Every line can be edited before you export, which matters when a product name or a price has to be exact. Read through the lines, fix the ones that came through wrong, then export.

steps.title: Export, then find the new version in Library

faq.q: Which style reads best on mobile?
faq.a: Bold type with a box or outline backdrop in the bottom third is the safest start, because it survives busy footage and pale backgrounds. Check the preview at Medium before going larger. Middle suits one short line.

faq.q: How long do the versions stay?
faq.a: Finished videos sit in the Library for 15 days, then expire, versions included. Download the cut you plan to post and keep your own copy of anything you reuse.
